answer: I'd like to describe a conversation with a complete stranger that I still think about. An interesting conversation I remember well was with an elderly man I happened to sit next to during a long train journey from Dhaka back to Sirajganj. It was about a year ago, and the train was delayed, so we had plenty of time. What began as polite small talk gradually turned into a genuinely [[fascinating]] discussion. He was a retired schoolteacher who had lived through decades of enormous change and shared stories that were both moving and eye-opening. He told me how, before the Jamuna bridge was built, crossing the river meant a long and unpredictable ferry journey, sometimes taking half a day. I found his perspective on life incredibly [[insightful]], shaped by experiences so different from my own. Time seemed to fly by as we talked about history, family and how much the world had changed. He was also curious about my work and asked me lots of questions about why so many young people want to study abroad. What made it so [[thought-provoking]] was how open and reflective he was with a complete stranger. By the end of the journey, I felt as though I had learned more than I would from any book. Honestly, that conversation reminded me how much wisdom ordinary people carry, if only we take the time to listen. It was a wonderfully [[enriching]] encounter, and it made me more willing to [[strike up]] conversations with people I do not know.

followUps.q: Do you often talk to strangers?
followUps.answer: More than I used to. On trains and buses I sometimes start a conversation if the other person seems friendly. Not everyone wants to chat, of course, so I try to read the situation first.

followUps.q: Who do you usually enjoy talking to the most?
followUps.answer: My grandfather, probably. He has a story for everything and a very dry sense of humour. Whenever we visit the village, I end up sitting with him for hours.

note: Set on a Dhaka to Sirajganj train; added the pre-bridge ferry memory and his questions about studying abroad; plain 'memorable' replaced by 'thought-provoking', added 'strike up'.
